DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Spring 2026 Menu Pricing Review

The price increases are reasonable, and the competitor check supports them. But the risotto proposal rests on a misreading of Table 1, which shows the risotto has the **highest** margin on the menu, not the weakest. The projection also leaves out the beef price rise flagged in Section 4. Together, these overstate the gain substantially.

## 1. The risotto has the highest margin, not the weakest

| Dish | Gross margin | Cash margin per plate | Plates per week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 | 310 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 | 260 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 | 180 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 | 120 |
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80%** | **£11.20** | **90** |
| Specials | 64% | various | 90 |

Section 5.2 says the risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu," and your summary repeats this. It has the **best** percentage margin, and its cash margin per plate is higher than the burger's or the curry's. It ties with specials for lowest sales.

Replacing it with a seasonal special at the same price, when specials average **64%**, would **cost about £200 a week** in gross profit at current volumes (16 points × £1,260 of risotto sales). The risotto may also be the only vegetarian main on the regular menu, which matters for group bookings.

Its low sales may be worth addressing through better menu placement, a description refresh or a recipe update. As it stands, though, the risotto is a strong performer per plate.

## 2. The beef price rise is left out of the projection

Section 4 notes a **12% beef increase from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start. The £810 a week projection treats food costs as unchanged. Steak and burger costs are mostly beef, so the effect could be up to:

| Dish | Current cost | Up to +12% | Per week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sirloin steak | £10.40 | about +£1.25 | about £150 |
| Beef burger | £4.20 | about +£0.50 | about £130 |
| **Total** | | | **up to about £280** |

On this basis, the steak's margin at £28 could actually *fall*, to about 58% from 60% now. Most of its £2 increase would be absorbed by the beef cost. Ask the chef for the beef share of each plate cost to firm up these figures.

## 3. Corrected projection

| | Per week | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| Price increases (as stated) | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less beef rise (upper estimate) | up to −£280 | up to −£14,560 |
| Less risotto swap | about −£200 | about −£10,400 |
| **Net** | **about £330–610** | **about £17,000–32,000** |

The lower end assumes the full beef increase and the risotto swap. Keeping the risotto brings the net to about £530–810 a week.

**Main-course margin:** The "about 71%" figure is correct arithmetic, but only for the named dishes, before the beef rise and without the risotto swap. Including both, it is nearer **68.5%**. That falls short of the 70% target rather than restoring it, and that target applies across all courses in any case.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Trading days:** The recommendation refers to "six trading days a week," but Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five**. Correct this.
- **Monitoring baseline:** Comparing spring volumes with January–February will mix up seasonal changes with price effects. Compare against the same weeks in 2025 if possible.
- **Evidence from the last price change:** "No visible effect on bookings" in 2024 is anecdotal. If you have the figures, include them.
- **Volume assumption:** "Volumes hold" is plausible, given that prices stay below the competitor midpoints. A downside case of 5% fewer plates on the three dishes would show how sensitive the gain is.

## 5. What holds up

- **Table 1 arithmetic** is correct throughout: margins, volumes (1,050 in total) and costs.
- **The competitor positioning is accurate.** All three new prices stay below the midpoint for that dish (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).
- **The £810 a week before costs** is correct: 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2.
- **The diagnosis is clear.** The margin has slipped from 70% to 67%, and prices haven't changed since September 2024.
- **Repeat custom of 60%** is a useful data point, although loyal regulars are also the guests most likely to *notice* price changes.

## Notes on the author's summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Each dish stays below the competitor midpoint | Correct |
| £810 a week, about £42,000 a year | Before the beef rise; about £330–610 a week after costs |
| Lifts main-course margin to about 71% | Before the beef rise and risotto swap; nearer 68.5% after |
| Risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu" | No, it has the highest (80%) |
| Replacing the risotto is "an easy improvement" | It would cost about £200 a week |
| Eight weeks of monitoring | Sensible, but use a seasonally matched baseline |

## Recommended changes

1. **Withdraw or rethink proposal 5.2.** Keep the risotto, or at least price any replacement to match its 80% margin.
2. **Include the beef increase** in the projection, using the actual beef share of plate costs.
3. **Reconsider the steak increase.** It may need to be higher than £2 to hold its margin, and there is room below the competitor midpoint of £29.50.
4. **Restate the margin projection**, and be clear about whether it refers to mains or all food.
5. **Change "six trading days" to "five,"** and use a year-on-year baseline for monitoring.
